newsitem.title: LATVIA: ANALYSIS - RTF, UNIBANKA SEEN AS BEST BET ON DULL BOURSE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS - RTF, UNIBANKA SEEN AS BEST BET ON DULL BOURSE.

text.p: Riga Transport Fleet and Unibanka are widely regarded as the only really interesting stocks on the Latvian bourse now and the jury is still out on newcomer Olainfarm, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday.

Like the market in neighbouring Lithuania, Latvia's galloped at a bullish pace early in the year, sparking optimism on the bourse. But analysts say that run was speculative, and once the bears bit, no red rags could be found to revive the bulls.
Trade volume has been low in recent months and prices have steadily fallen. In the last week, the Rietumu index has dropped to 149.4 from 153.93.
"Right now, only Unibanka and the Riga Transport Fleet (RTF) are really interesting...RTF looks relatively cheap," said one analyst.
"Unibanka and RTF are the most attractive shares," said Artis Goba, a dealer with Saules Bank.
"RTF is not just short-term and speculative but it has long-term potential...its results last year were not very good, but it is well managed and looks like it will make a profit this year," he said.
"Unibanka looks like a bank for the future...it is stable and won't have any big problems," he added.
Dealers remain divided over pharmaceutical producer Olainfarm, which bounced up and down since its debut last week.
Some dealers say its poor first quarter results do not reflect the real picture and that it has lots of potential.
Others are far less bullish and say that it is not very profitable.
"Its first half results will give a better indication of the direction it is heading in," said one dealer.
The general outlook for the bourse is dull.
"There is no fresh money in the market...most of it is being channeled into privatisation certificates," said Leonid Ruderman of Parekss Bank.
"Ventspils Nafta and some other big companies are to be privatised and that's where the money is going now," he said.
Big companies, or the lack of them, are seen as a key obstacle to the development of the market.
Market capitalisation is only five percent of GDP, compared to around 22 percent in Estonia and 18 percent in Lithuania.
"In Latvia, we are talking about a very small market with very few shares," one analyst told Reuters.
"Most of the companies are very small and there simply are not enough of them," he said.
Poor transparancy is viewed as another problem.
"Most of the companies are not really interested in publishing their results...they only do the minimum required of them by the bourse," said Ruderman.

"There is a big difference between Latvian accounting standards and international standards, and most of the companies' quarterly results are based on Latvian standards...which do not give a clear picture," he said.
"Some of the bigger companies base their annual results on international standards, but Unibanka is the only listing whose balance sheet consistently gives an accurate picture," he said.
"The market is not reacting to news the way you would expect," said the analyst.
"This is partly because of poor rules of disclosure, and partly because there are not enough local players," he said.

"You basically have some brokers doing deals for a few foreign investors...there are no local investment or portfolio funds and the insurance companies have not begun to seriously invest in equities," he added.
